lines.show: Most cancer drugs fail before they reach a patient.
Part of the problem is the testing.
For decades, cancer cells have been grown flat, in a plastic dish.
Real tumours aren't flat.
So labs now grow something closer to the real thing: tiny 3D copies of a patient's tumour, called organoids.
This year, two leading cancer centres used organoids to switch off every gene, one at a time, and find the ones a cancer can't live without.
Hundreds of genes mattered more in organoids than in flat cells, and those are now being put forward as drug targets.
Here's the catch.
Organoids change two things at once.
One is the shape. 3D instead of flat.
The other is the food.
Cells in a dish live in a liquid called the medium.
Flat cells usually get serum, the nutrient-rich part of blood.
Organoids get a clean, lab-made medium with almost no cholesterol.
So when a gene matters more in an organoid, which change caused it?
The shape, which is the whole point?
Or just the diet?
The data to tell them apart already existed.
A big public database had flat cells grown on the organoid medium.
Same diet, no 3D shape.
If a gene matters more there too, the shape can't explain it. The food can.
We ran that check on all 17,525 genes.
456 clearly behave differently in organoids.
So how many of those 456 also change when the only thing you change is the food?
If organoids were finding something new, that number should be small.
Eighty-five percent.
Here's why that matters.
These are exactly the kind of genes being put forward as new drug targets.
But for most of them, ordinary flat cells show the same change, as soon as they get the same food.
So the effect may not come from the tumour's 3D shape at all. It may come from what we feed it.
And in a patient, a tumour is fed by blood, which is full of cholesterol.
So a weakness that only shows up on a diet with almost no cholesterol may not exist in the patient at all.
On this chart, each dot is one of those genes.
If a dot sits on the dashed line, flat cells on organoid food changed it just as much as the organoid did.
Most of them sit right on that line.
The clearest case is cholesterol.
Organoid food has almost none, so the cells have to make their own. That makes the genes that build it, like SQLE, suddenly look essential.
That leaves 69 genes that don't clearly follow the food.
For 68 of them, the data can't say either way.
Just one leans toward the shape, and not strongly.
Three of them, SCAP, DDX3X and ITGB1, were among Sanger's top picks.
They're the more credible leads: the ones still worth chasing.
This is a pattern in existing data, not proof.
But there's a simple way to check.
Put the cholesterol back into the organoid's food.
If these genes stop mattering, it was the food. If they still matter, they're stronger candidates.
It takes about two weeks, and no new screen.
We also tried hard to prove ourselves wrong.
We checked the result on patient samples the analysis had never seen.
We reran it 150 times on reshuffled data.
Five rounds of independent review checked the code and the claims.
And when one early finding didn't hold up, we dropped it.
All of this is free at itsthemedium.com.
Look up any gene and get a simple answer: does it follow the food, or not?
Researchers can paste their own list of genes and see in seconds which ones look like diet effects.
Muse, Meta's AI model, is the research assistant.
Ask it a question and it searches the full table with its own tools, shows every step, and links every gene to the data.
And Muse ran the research loop behind this whole audit.
Organoids are still a big step forward.
We just need to check what we're feeding them.
It's the Medium.
